As context windows grew larger in 2024, as much as 1 million tokens 
in some models, many teams began to ask whether retrieval systems 
were still necessary. If a model can process very large inputs, you 
may consider passing entire document collections directly into 
the prompt and relying on the model to reason over them.
When you deploy systems this way, the tradeoffs appear quickly. Each query 
reprocesses the full context, driving up token costs and increasing lat

sses the full context, driving up token costs and increasing latency. 
Longer prompts also reduce consistency, as models struggle to reliably 
focus on the few details that actually matter. Once query volume increases, 
retrieval becomes necessary to control cost, latency, and response quality.
Larger context windows have not removed retrieval from the system. 
Instead, they have changed how you design it. Modern RAG pipelines rely 
on multiple components that each handle a specific responsibility. You brea

components that each handle a specific responsibility. You break 
documents into retrievable units, encode text into numerical representations, 
search efficiently across large collections, and use rerankers to prioritize 
the most relevant results before generation. Together, these components 
allow the system to meet the demands of real production environments.
This book focuses on the technical foundations you need to 
build RAG systems that perform reliably in practice. You will learn

how to give models access to more information than they could hold in context.
